chapter_theme: Fullness of character: the worthy hold all good qualities as their own, rest on five pillars, don't tell others' faults, and do good to those who harm them. This fullness doesn't depend on poverty or wealth, and the chapter finally places the earth's stability upon it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the qualities suited to fullness in general (981-982), and specific ones (983-987), the excellence of those filled with them (988-990).

981.reading: For those who know what is fitting and take on fullness of character, all that is good is said to be கடன்.

positions.position: கடன் means what is natural: all good qualities are inherent, otherwise the word சான்றாண்மை wouldn't apply.
கடன் means duty, and all efforts made to fulfil it count as good duties.

982.reading: The goodness of the worthy is the goodness of character; any other goodness isn't counted among goodnesses at all.
982.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் as bodily good looks, and says it doesn't even appear in the lists of goods such as birth and learning. Kalaignar also has அழகு. The verse's own பிற is open, and a stronger reading dismisses everything other than character.

983.reading: Love, shame, fellow-feeling, kindly regard and truthfulness: these five are the pillars planted to bear worth.
983.nuance: Four of the five are about how one regards other people. Parimelazhagar stretches two of them: love extends beyond kin, and truth holds everywhere. Their absence makes worth fall, not merely diminish.

984.reading: Austerity has the goodness of not killing, and worth has the goodness of not telling others' evil.
984.nuance: The verse sets speech at the level of the ascetic's non-violence. Talking of another's fault is thus the moral equivalent of what killing is for a tapas. Kalaignar makes the silence cover harm done by others, which leaves open how it fits with exposing wrongdoing.

985.reading: The strength of those who accomplish is to bow; that is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes around.
985.nuance: படை and மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் use the language of war, and the pun is that a foe (மாற்றார்) gets changed (மாற்றும்), not destroyed. Parimelazhagar makes the bowing concrete and strategic: stooping to gather allies.

986.reading: If asked what the touchstone of worth is, it is accepting defeat even from those who aren't one's equal.
986.nuance: Parimelazhagar specifies that one accepts it while able to win. Without that, the verse describes mere loss. The defeat then lifts one above the other person, an inversion of the usual sense of victory.

987.reading: If you don't do what is sweet even to those who have done you harm, what has worth brought?
987.nuance: A demanding test is framed as a question about use: worth is judged by what it produces in the hardest case.

988.reading: Poverty is no disgrace for one who has the firmness called worth.
988.nuance: திண்மை makes worth a hardness able to bear pressure. The verse doesn't call poverty good, only that it doesn't carry the disgrace it otherwise would.

989.reading: Those called the ஆழி of worth won't shift even when the age shifts.
989.nuance: ஊழி and ஆழி chime. The cosmic dissolution is a scale reference for constancy.

positions.position: ஆழி means shore: worth is the sea, and they are what holds it in when other seas overflow.
ஆழி means sea: they stand as the sea that doesn't change when all seas are overturned.

990.reading: If the worthy decline in worth, the great earth itself will not bear its load.
990.nuance: Parimelazhagar says both events are impossible, so this is a thought experiment showing their dependence. He also reports a reading in which the worthy are the earth's helpers in bearing. Kalaignar reads பொறை as the world's forbearance: it won't patiently tolerate their decline.

links.note: Chapters 97 and 99 give different answers to humiliation. 967 prefers being called dead to living behind those who scorn you, and 986 makes accepting defeat even from lesser people the touchstone of worth. The two make most sense as distinct ideals, honour and fullness of character, and not as one code.

988 says poverty brings no disgrace to one with worth. 1044 says poverty produces degraded speech even in the well-born. Whether character can hold against poverty is answered one way here and the other in the chapter on poverty.

151 holds up the earth, bearing those who dig it, as the model of forbearance for people. 990 reverses the dependence: the earth's own bearing relies on the worthy. The model has become the dependent.
Two images of bearing a load form a stack: five qualities are pillars carrying worth, and worth carries what the earth bears. The chapter's architecture rests the world on small daily dispositions.
The formula ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் recurs. In 225 this strength is enduring hunger, ranked below relieving it, and in 985 it is bowing. The Kural keeps redefining strength as some form of restraint.
314 says one punishes those who harm by doing them good until they are ashamed, and 987 makes that same return a test of whether worth has any use. 314 gives it a purpose, and 987 makes it a measure.
261 defines austerity as enduring pain and not hurting living things. 984 picks out not killing as its core, in order to place not speaking of others' faults at the same rank for worth.

source_issues: 988: the Parimelazhagar text runs on into the gloss for 989; only the part before சான்றாண்மைக்கு ஆழி was used.
986, 990: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss, so it may not be independent. 981 and 989 are also very close to it.
987: Parimelazhagar's text lacks the usual opening of the விளக்கம் section.
988 and 989: the Parimelazhagar texts cite the same Purananuru line by different numbers (350 and 330).
989: Pope's couplet has 'the fates should fail' for ஊழி பெயரினும, while the commentators read a change of age.
